To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) immigrants catch up with native workers over time, but the speed of the catch-up varies by immigrant group; (2) the second generation of immigrants performs on average worse that the children of natives, but this is due to differences in socio-economic backgrounds, and not to the fact of being children of immigrants; (3) the differences in wages by country of origin of immigrants are strongly correlated across host countries, and this is due to immigrants of the same country of origin receiving different returns
the immigrant wage gap is driven by immigrants gaining access better paying firms and that immigrants from the same country of origin have similar labour market outcomes across host countries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms driving immigrant economic assimilation and with the factors affecting immigrant labour market performance.
the labour market integration and economic assimilation of immigrant populations and their children, in particular in the host countries.
the labour market integration and performance of immigrants and their second-generation in the host country, and how these are shaped by differences in country-of-origin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

immigrants are not a homogenous group, and that the labour market performance and the degree of assimilation of immigrants and their descendants vary widely depending on their socio-economic characteristics and the host country.
the labour market integration process is driven by the same factors in the first and second generation and that these factors are similar across host countries.
immigrants are not a homogeneous group, but rather a diverse group of people with very different backgrounds and characteristics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the labour market integration process of immigrants in host countries can be divided into two distinct stages.
immigrants and their children face a number of hurdles in the host countries.
the immigrant wage gap is driven by differences in socio- economic background, differences in returns to education and differences in the quality of the immigrant population.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the labour market performance differences across immigrant populations are largely explained by differences in education and that these differences are largely driven by differences in education returns across immigrant populations.
the labour market performance immigrants and their children is largely determined by the same mechanisms in all host countries.
immigrants are able to overcome their initial disadvantages and integrate in the labour market, but that the extent of their integration varies by country of origin.
